title: Success Comes From Agency, Not Slogans
author: Make Work Better
summary: This article opens with Unilever CEO Fernando Fernandez's attempt to implant strategic priorities by making employees chant financial metrics before meetings, and uses it as a launching point to argue that performance culture achieved through slogans, jargon, and top-down mandates fails -- and that the only genuine performance culture is a high-agency culture in disguise. The author draws on a 2018 MIT finding that only 28% of executives and middle managers could list their company's strategic objectives, noting that shouting financial jargon at frontline employees only compounds this problem without addressing it. The deeper point, drawing on Martin Seligman's forthcoming book Agency, is that human progress occurs not when everyone follows orders but when people are empowered to have autonomy-imbued impact themselves. The author contrasts Unilever's approach with Ritz-Carlton (employees can spend $1,000 to solve a customer problem without permission) and Octopus Energy (any employee can solve any customer's problem on the first call). The argument is that when you treat people as adults, explain the business to them, and give them the tools to solve problems, performance takes care of itself -- no margin-expansion chants required.
points: * The MIT 2018 finding -- that only 28% of executives and middle managers could list their company's strategic objectives -- exposes the actual problem behind performance-culture sloganeering: the priorities of the top team are not top of mind for workers lower down, and barking financial jargon at the frontline makes this worse, not better. * The Seligman Agency insight reframes the leader's role: human progress occurs not through ordered compliance but through empowered autonomy -- leaders who try to drive results by telling workers to pursue 'positive growth margin expansion in hard currency' are working against the psychological conditions under which people actually produce excellent work. * The Ritz-Carlton and Octopus Energy examples operationalize high-agency culture: giving a frontline employee the ability to spend $1,000 to solve a customer problem without seeking permission communicates trust, aligns authority with responsibility, and produces better customer outcomes than any jargon-driven mandate. * The causal mechanism matters: you make businesses more successful by creating the conditions for success, not by ordering improvement -- results are achieved indirectly, through the structural and relational conditions that enable effective action, not through exhortation. * The diagnostic the article offers is simple: when you hear opaque corporate values or strategic jargon being used to drive performance, ask what would actually be helpful right now -- what obstacle needs to be removed, what authority needs to be granted, what trust needs to be signaled -- because the performance culture you want is a high-agency culture in disguise.
quotes: 'Before saying hello I say: Volume growth, positive mix, consistent growth margin expansion for profit growth in hard currency' -- this is Unilever's CEO Fernando Fernandez's dystopian attempt to implant his strategic priorities in his employees' minds.

In 2018 researchers at MIT found that only 28% of executives and middle managers could list their company's strategic objectives. Top bosses get preoccupied that no one understands their priorities. But barking financial jargon at the frontline is a little like telling children to be happier.

Improved results are achieved indirectly. We make businesses more successful by creating the conditions for success, not by ordering improvement. It's why the most important thing that these bosses can do is create high agency cultures, freeing people up to have impact in their own roles.
Seligman makes one point emphatically, that human progress occurs, not when we have everyone following orders, but when you empower everyone to have an autonomy-imbued impact themselves.

When you treat people like adults, explain the business to them and give them the tools to solve problems you don't need to yell about margin expansion in hard currency. The performance takes care of itself. The most effective performance culture is high-agency culture in disguise.
